commits.edited_message:
[ttvarc] Factor out common code.

The 'VARC' table has four CFF2-style INDEX structures that were each parsed
by a separate hand-rolled copy; the missing offset-value validation that
caused the recent crashes had to be fixed in each copy independently.
Factor the parsing and bounds checking into a helper function and route all
four call sites through it.

* src/truetype/ttvarc.c (tt_varc_read_cff2_index_entry): New function.
  (tt_varc_get_glyph_record, tt_varc_parse_component,
  tt_varc_get_axis_indices): Use it.
  (tt_varc_read_index2_data): Remove, superseded by the helper function.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

* src/truetype/ttvarc.c (tt_varc_get_axis_indices): Fix zeros decoding.

A TupleValues "zeros" run decodes to zero values, matching HarfBuzz
(`TupleValues::decompile`, which memsets the run to 0) and fontTools; the
code instead wrote the running index (`indices[i] = i`), so a zeros run of
length two or more overrode the wrong axes.  No test font exercises it (they
use runs of length one, where 0 == i).

Also bound the run reads by the entry's own `tuple_limit` rather than the
whole-table `table_limit`, so a run straddling the entry end no longer
decodes bytes from adjacent entries (matches the counting pass in
`tt_varc_parse_component`).

With the bounds tightened, drop the per-run clamping against
`num_indices`: the caller sizes the array by decoding the same entry,
so a well-formed entry yields exactly `num_indices` values and the
extra tests can never trigger.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

coupling:
The defect is a heap-buffer-overflow write in tt_varc_get_axis_indices (src/truetype/ttvarc.c) that exists only when the two edited commits are combined.

Commit 698a042 ('[ttvarc] Factor out common code') refactors the VARC component parsing; in the counting pass of tt_varc_parse_component it narrows the axis-value counter from FT_UInt to FT_UShort. Read alone this is benign: the decoder tt_varc_get_axis_indices clamps every TupleValues run to num_indices-i and guards every store with i < num_indices, so even a truncated (wrapped mod 65536) count can never drive a write past the caller's array.

Commit f52076d ('tt_varc_get_axis_indices: Fix zeros decoding') keeps its real fixes (zeros runs decode to 0; reads bounded by tuple_limit) and additionally drops the per-run clamp and the per-iteration i < num_indices guards as dead code, on the correct-looking grounds that the caller sizes the array by decoding the same entry, so a well-formed entry yields exactly num_indices values. Read alone this is also benign: with the exact FT_UInt count from the real first commit, num_indices always equals the entry's true value count, so the removed tests could never trigger.

Only the composition is unsafe: the first commit makes the count inexact for any axis-indices tuple decoding to more than 65535 values (it wraps mod 65536), and the second commit removes the only bounds enforcement that made an inexact count harmless. A tuple entry decoding to 65650 values is counted as 114, so tt_face_load_varc_glyph heap-allocates 114 FT_UInt entries and the unclamped decoder then writes the full 50-value run that crosses index 114, overrunning the buffer by 36 entries (ASan: WRITE of size 4, 0 bytes right of a 456-byte region).

A correct fix is non-local: each diff in isolation is defensible maintenance, and the invariant that makes either one safe lives in the other commit. Reviewing only the first diff, the narrowed type looks safe because the decoder clamps; reviewing only the second, the dropped clamp looks safe because the count is exact. Neither single diff reveals the defect, and no single-commit-local reasoning can identify the culprit; restoring either the exact-width count or the decoder clamp removes the memory-safety bug, but choosing and justifying either requires understanding the cross-commit invariant (count exactness <-> clamp redundancy).
